options.text: By altering the amino acid sequence of the protein the gene codes for
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By changing blood flow to the tissue
options.explanation: Blood flow is not the taught route.
Membranes are not altered by gene changes.
Temperature plays no part in the chain.

questions.stem: What are the three ways a base sequence can change?

options.explanation: Those are mitosis contexts.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Those are normal cell processes, not mutations.
None of these is the taught mutation list.

questions.stem: In an insertion, what happens to the groups of three bases downstream?

options.explanation: Deletion is a separate mutation kind.
Regrouping, not simple reversal, is the effect.

options.text: They are regrouped, so the amino acids they code for change
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The frame shift touches every later triplet.

questions.stem: How many bases does one codon contain?

options.explanation: Two bases cannot specify twenty amino acids.
The reading frame uses triplets.
That number belongs to chromosome pairs.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: Why does one inserted base damage more than one amino acid position?

options.text: The reading frame shifts, so every later triplet is read differently
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The inserted base persists.
That describes substitution, not insertion.

options.text: The cell repairs the rest instantly
options.explanation: No instant repair is part of the account.

questions.stem: Define an insertion mutation.
questions.modelAnswer: A fresh base lands at a random spot in the DNA string, changing the amino acid coded there and regrouping every triplet after it.

questions.stem: State the link between codons and amino acids.
questions.modelAnswer: Each group of three bases, one codon, codes for one amino acid in the protein.

questions.stem: Explain why a single inserted base alters several amino acids, not just one.
questions.modelAnswer: The cell reads the sequence in consecutive triplets, so inserting one base pushes every later base across a boundary and regroups all following codons.

questions.stem: A mutation adds one base near the start of a gene that is 300 bases long. Describe the extent of the protein damage you would expect.
questions.modelAnswer: The reading frame shifts from the insertion onward, so nearly every codon after that point is regrouped and most of the downstream amino acid sequence changes.

questions.stem: What does a deletion mutation remove?

options.explanation: The mutation targets bases, not backbone parts.

options.text: A base from the DNA sequence
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Chromosome loss is not the taught deletion.
Amino acids are consequences, not what is removed.

questions.stem: Which mutation type changes only the amino acid of its own triplet?

options.explanation: Deletions shift every later triplet.
Neither keeps the frame intact.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Insertions shift every later triplet.

questions.stem: Why do insertion and deletion share the knock-on effect?

options.explanation: Deletion removes material.
Neither deletes whole codons directly.
Triplets are exactly what they disturb.

options.text: Both shift the grouping of every later triplet
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A substitution swaps A for G inside one codon. How many amino acids change at most?

options.text: One, the amino acid that codon specifies
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The frame survives a substitution.
The swapped codon may code differently.
Only the affected triplet is read differently.

questions.stem: Which mutated sequence type keeps every later triplet aligned?

options.explanation: Neither preserves the grouping.

options.text: A substitution, since the base count is unchanged
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The count grows, so alignment breaks.
The count drops, so alignment breaks.

questions.stem: Define a substitution mutation.
questions.modelAnswer: A base is randomly swapped for a different base, changing at most the amino acid of the triplet containing it.

questions.stem: State the effect shared by insertion and deletion mutations.
questions.modelAnswer: Both regroup the triplets downstream, changing the amino acids those codons specify.

questions.stem: Explain why substitution lacks the knock-on effect that insertion causes.
questions.modelAnswer: Substitution replaces one base with another and leaves the base count intact, so the triplet boundaries downstream stay exactly where they were.

questions.stem: Two mutations hit the same gene: one deletes a base early on, another swaps one base near the end. State which mutation is likely to damage more of the protein and why.
questions.modelAnswer: The deletion damages more, because removing a base regroups every later triplet, whereas the substitution only risks the single amino acid of its own codon.

questions.stem: What is the most common effect of a genetic mutation on the phenotype?

options.explanation: Most mutations leave the phenotype unchanged.
Benefit is even rarer than harm.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Lethality is rare, not the common case.

questions.stem: Why can a mutation be significant for an enzyme?

options.explanation: Mutations can alter any protein, enzymes included.
Substrates are chemicals, not genes.
Most do nothing; some harm.

options.text: A reshaped active site may fail to bind its substrate
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which condition is given as an example of a harmful mutation?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

Scurvy is a vitamin deficiency, not a mutation.

questions.stem: When can a new phenotype spread through a population?

options.explanation: Advantageous phenotypes do spread.

options.text: When it grants a survival or reproductive advantage
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Neutral or harmful changes do not spread by selection.
The rule covers animals too.

questions.stem: A mutation makes a bird's feathers more attractive to mates. What follows?

options.explanation: Advantage keeps alleles in play.
Spread takes generations.

options.text: That allele is more likely to be passed to future generations
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The bird must change its own DNA again
options.explanation: The allele is already there.

questions.stem: Summarise the three levels of mutation effect on phenotype.
questions.modelAnswer: Most mutations have no effect, some have a small effect, and rarely a mutation has a significant effect.

questions.stem: Give the example of a significant harmful mutation taught here.
questions.modelAnswer: Sickle cell anaemia, from a mutated haemoglobin gene.

questions.stem: Explain why most mutations are silent at the phenotype level.
questions.modelAnswer: The altered protein usually keeps its shape and function, so the organism's observable characteristics barely change and the mutation passes unnoticed.

questions.stem: A mutation slightly alters an enzyme without abolishing its activity. Classify this outcome on the taught effect ladder.
questions.modelAnswer: It sits in the band where some mutations have a small effect, since the protein shape is mildly changed and its function is only slightly affected.

questions.stem: Do mutations need a cause like radiation to occur?

options.explanation: Spontaneous mutation happens without radiation.
Chemicals raise the rate; they are not required.
Spontaneous occurrence is the baseline.

options.text: No, they arise spontaneously and continuously anyway
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Which of these is ionising radiation?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That is a chemical mutagen.
Sound does not ionise.
Sugar is not radiation at all.

questions.stem: How does ionising radiation raise the mutation rate?

options.explanation: Base-level damage is the taught route.

options.text: It damages bonds and changes base sequences
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Melting is not the taught mechanism.
Protein is not added by radiation.

questions.stem: Which everyday exposure is named as a chemical mutagen source?

options.explanation: No such example is taught.
Water is not a mutagen here.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Sunlight is the radiation case.

questions.stem: Why are mutagens linked to cancer?

options.explanation: They damage cells.
The taught link runs through mutations.
Body cells are affected too.

options.text: Higher mutation rates can push cells into uncontrolled division
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: List the mutagenic exposures taught in this note.
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma rays, x-rays, ultraviolet rays, and chemical mutagens such as the chemicals in tobacco.

questions.stem: State what ionising radiation does to DNA.
questions.modelAnswer: It damages bonds and causes changes in base sequences.

questions.stem: Explain why the same mutagens appear in cancer-prevention advice.
questions.modelAnswer: By raising the mutation rate in body cells, ionising radiation and chemical mutagens increase the chance of the mutations that make cells cancerous, so limiting exposure lowers that risk.

questions.stem: A worker moves from an office job to outdoor fieldwork with strong sunshine. State which mutagen exposure rises and what cellular risk increases with it.
questions.modelAnswer: Ultraviolet exposure from sunshine rises, and with a higher mutation rate in skin cells the risk of mutations that lead to cancer increases too.
